I've been working this land for 45 years and I know Quzhou's soils and rhythms well. With only two of us at home and my son working in the city, I need to keep things manageable. My 8 mu runs the full wheat-maize rotation — same ground, two crops a year. Here's how I'll handle it:

**Winter Wheat:** I'll plant improved variety Jimai 22 — I've grown it for years and it performs reliably here. I'll do rotary tillage after maize harvest to break up the compaction and incorporate stubble. Base fertilizer goes in before sowing: phosphorus and potassium together with about half the nitrogen. I'll top-dress at jointing. Total nitrogen around 14 kg/mu — I've cut back from what I used to apply after attending that county extension seminar a few years ago. Three irrigations: pre-winter freeze, jointing, and heading. That's usually enough unless we get a dry spring. Two pesticide passes — one herbicide in winter, one fungicide before heading for stripe rust, which has been a problem here.

**Summer Maize:** Right after wheat harvest I'll direct seed Zhengdan 958 with no-tillage — saves my back and keeps moisture in. The summer rains usually cover most of water needs, but I'll irrigate twice: once at emergence if it's dry, once at tasseling. I apply nitrogen in two splits — some at planting, the rest at the 10-leaf stage. I'll spray herbicide early post-emergence and watch for corn borer around silking for a second application.

With off-farm income coming in, I'm not desperate to maximize every jin, but I still want respectable yields to justify the inputs.

Nitrogen rates are moderate and split-applied based on decades of local soil knowledge and extension guidance, reflecting a farmer who has deliberately rationalized inputs downward from earlier high-application practices. Pesticide applications are minimal but targeted: herbicide plus fungicide for wheat, herbicide plus corn borer control for maize. Off-farm household income reduces pressure to push yields at the cost of higher input spending or labor burden."
